prompt_text: Summarize the dispute over renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America", including who is proposing it and who is objecting, and explain the current state of that debate as of today.

results.response:
## As of August 29, 2026

**This is no longer merely a proposal.** President Donald Trump first floated “Lake America” during an escalating trade dispute with Canada, then signed an executive order on **August 27, 2026**, directing the Interior Department and U.S. Board on Geographic Names to replace “Lake Ontario” in federal maps, databases, contracts and communications. The administration says the name recognizes the lake’s importance to American history, commerce and Great Lakes investment. ([whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/honoring-the-american-history-of-the-great-lakes-and-renaming-lake-ontario-as-lake-america-3a36/?utm_source=openai))

### Who is objecting?

- **Canada:** Prime Minister **Mark Carney** and Ontario Premier **Doug Ford** reject the change. They emphasize that “Ontario” comes from an Indigenous Wendat/Huron name that predates both countries and say Canada will continue calling it Lake Ontario. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/3ac58dca0ca83c15605d4dbff146b28a))
- **The Seneca Nation:** President **J. Conrad Seneca** has demanded that Trump rescind the order, calling it cultural erasure and “blatant disrespect.” He also argues that it violates the spirit of the **1794 Treaty of Canandaigua** between the United States and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1f5f831ab8d79d18a38999328a1af8c2))
- **New York officials:** Governor **Kathy Hochul** says New York will not use “Lake America.” Democratic congressional leaders, including Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, have criticized the renaming as a distraction from the economic costs of the Canada trade conflict. ([ny1.com](https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/news/2026/08/28/trump-s-lake-ontario-rename-draws-criticism-from-new-york-leaders?utm_source=openai))
- **Congressional Democrats:** Reps. **Tim Kennedy** and **Debbie Dingell** are preparing legislation to reverse or counter the order, although Republican control of Congress makes passage difficult. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/08/27/trump-lake-ontario-america-democrats-bill))

### Where things stand

For **U.S. federal-government purposes**, “Lake America” is taking effect: Interior issued an implementing order, and USGS says future publications will use the new name. ([edit.doi.gov](https://edit.doi.gov/document-library/secretary-order/so-3453-lake-america))

But Trump cannot require **Canada, New York State, private mapmakers, news organizations or ordinary citizens** to adopt it. There is also no single international authority capable of imposing one universal name for a shared body of water. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/3ac58dca0ca83c15605d4dbff146b28a))

**Bottom line:** The federal government now calls it “Lake America,” while Canada, New York, Indigenous leaders and other opponents continue to recognize “Lake Ontario.” The dispute therefore remains an unresolved political and diplomatic naming conflict—not a universally accepted renaming.

## The Dispute Over Renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America"

**Who's proposing it and why:**

President Donald Trump announced he was giving "serious consideration" to renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America," mirroring his move to rename the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America early in his second term. The proposal is tied directly to the broader U.S.-Canada trade conflict: Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" on Thursday, following through on his threat over the lake after U.S.-Canada trade negotiations collapsed. The collapse triggered 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, with Canada announcing matching tariffs set to take effect Sept. 8.

Trump previewed the move on social media, once writing that America doesn't "expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer," and posting images showing the lake renamed "Lake America."

**The formal action:**

The White House's presidential action directs that within 30 days, the Secretary of the Interior shall, in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names, take all appropriate actions to rename as "Lake America" the body of water currently named as Lake Ontario, bounded on the south and east by New York, and on the north, west, and southwest by Ontario. The order also states that the Secretary shall update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) to reflect the renaming and remove all references to Lake Ontario from the GNIS.

Trump's justification leans on geography and history: with the deepest parts of the lake's waters lying within U.S. territory, the administration argues the U.S. claims most of the lake's volume, and that the lake has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense. By the numbers, roughly 47% of the lake that straddles the border with Ontario lies within the U.S.

At the signing, Trump remarked, "The lake change -- 'Lake of America' -- was something I've been thinking about for a long time," and when pressed on the message behind it, said, he has "no message," but added, "No message, as you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly."

**Who's objecting:**

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney led the pushback, noting the name's deep historical roots. He wrote that the name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari'io, meaning "the lake is beautiful, the lake is big," and that the name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States. Carney added pointedly, "We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms," and concluded that "Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always."

Beyond the political objection, there's also a practical/legal limit to the move: Trump has wide latitude over how the US government refers to geographic landmarks, but he can't force other countries to follow suit. Media and mapping companies are also resisting — for example, MapQuest says it will not rename Lake Ontario in its services despite Trump's executive order. This echoes the earlier Gulf of Mexico situation, where the attempt to rename the gulf drew international opposition, and numerous media outlets vowed to stick with the common and internationally recognized usage.

**Current state of the debate (as of August 29, 2026):**

The order is now signed and, per Trump, already in effect: "This is official, effective immediately," Trump said after signing the order, adding that he'd "filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else" for the name change and that "We notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So we've done everything that you have to do, and this is official, effective immediately." Practically, the order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and his department to update the Geographic Names Information System within 30 days and requires all federal government references to the lake to use "Lake America."

However, the dispute is far from settled: Canada rejects the renaming outright and continues to call it Lake Ontario, tensions remain elevated amid the tariff war (with Canadian retaliatory tariffs set to hit September 8), and non-government entities like mapping services are declining to adopt the new name — meaning "Lake America" currently exists as official U.S. federal nomenclature only, with no international recognition and active pushback both diplomatically and commercially.

The dispute over renaming Lake Ontario to **"Lake America"** centers around an executive action issued by U.S. President Donald Trump amid escalating trade and political tensions between the United States and Canada. 

---

### The Proposal
* **The Proposer:** U.S. President Donald Trump and the White House.
* **The Action:** On August 27, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order directing U.S. federal agencies—including the Department of the Interior—to update official maps, documents, geographic databases, and communications to refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America".
* **The Rationale:** The administration framed the renaming as a recognition of American economic prominence, security contributions, and investments in the Great Lakes (such as U.S. Coast Guard icebreaking operations), alongside rhetoric surrounding an escalating trade dispute with Canada.

---

### Who Is Objecting
The proposal has faced broad opposition across international, state, municipal, and Indigenous leadership:

1. **The Canadian Government:**
   * Prime Minister Mark Carney and Canadian officials dismissed the move, with Carney emphasizing that Canadians will know the body of water as *"Lake Ontario – then, now and always"*.
   * Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and various Ontario municipal leaders characterized the move as an ineffective political distraction with no standing in Canada.

2. **New York State and Local Officials:**
   * **State Leadership:** New York Governor Kathy Hochul called the order "patently absurd" and criticized the administration for diverting focus from substantive domestic issues.
   * **Local Municipalities:** The City Council of Rochester, New York (the largest U.S. city situated on the lake) passed a unanimous proclamation condemning the move and resolved that the city will continue to officially recognize only the name Lake Ontario.
   * **U.S. Lawmakers:** Congressional Democrats announced plans to introduce legislation aimed at blocking or overturning the federal name change.

3. **Indigenous Leaders:**
   * Indigenous representatives, including Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca, condemned the renaming. They highlighted that the name *Ontario* originates from the Iroquoian language (often translated as "great lake" or "sparkling water") and argued that the unilateral name change disrespects Indigenous heritage and violates long-standing historical treaties.

---

### Current State of the Debate
* **Jurisdictional Limits:** Because Lake Ontario is an international body of water divided by the U.S.–Canada border, the U.S. President has no authority to alter how Canada or international maritime bodies designate the lake. Canada’s Geographical Names Board maintains the official name as **Lake Ontario / Lac Ontario**.
* **Federal vs. Local Implementation:** While U.S. federal agencies are subject to the executive order for official federal publications and mapping, New York state bodies, local municipalities along the shoreline, and tribal nations have stated they will ignore the order and continue using "Lake Ontario".
* **Pending Pushback:** The debate remains an active political friction point, with U.S. lawmakers drafting counter-legislation and Canadian and cross-border officials treating the executive order primarily as a political stunt rather than a permanent geographic reality.

**In August 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump proposed and then formally directed a name change for Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as a jab amid an escalating U.S.-Canada trade war (following collapsed talks and new tariffs).** This applies only to U.S. federal government usage and has no force internationally or on Canada.[[1]](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgwdn1g58yo)

Trump floated the idea on August 25, 2026, via Truth Social, citing reduced expected business with Ontario, then signed Executive Order “Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America” on August 27. He described it as something he had considered “for a long time,” compared it to his earlier “Gulf of America” renaming of the Gulf of Mexico, and suggested possibly renaming oceans next. The order claims the U.S. holds most of the lake’s volume and deepest parts, highlights its economic role (jobs, commerce, infrastructure), and directs the Interior Secretary and U.S. Board on Geographic Names to update federal databases (like the Geographic Names Information System) and all executive-branch maps, documents, and communications within 30 days, removing prior “Lake Ontario” references where consistent with law. U.S. Geological Survey and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency systems were updated quickly, including NGA’s Geographic Names Server by August 29. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum supported it. The lake (smallest Great Lake by surface area) is shared, with roughly 52-53% of its surface in Canada (Ontario province) and the rest in New York. The original name derives from an Indigenous Iroquoian/Wendat word (Ontari’io or similar), often translated as “great lake,” “beautiful lake,” or “lake of shining waters,” in use since the 17th century and predating both nations. A 1989 U.S.-Canada naming agreement favored retaining established names.[[2]](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/27/politics/trump-rename-lake-america)

**Objectors include Canadian officials, some U.S. state leaders, Indigenous groups, scientists, Democrats, and much of the public.** Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected it immediately, stating the name (from the Wendat) is over 400 years old and that “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.” Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston, and others echoed this, calling it “foolishness” and affirming the name “now and forever.” New York Governor Kathy Hochul (whose state borders the lake) said New York would not use the new name; other U.S. governors (e.g., Michigan’s Gretchen Whitmer, Wisconsin’s Tony Evers, who mocked it by “renaming” Lake Michigan on a napkin, Vermont’s Phil Scott) denounced it. Indigenous nations like the Seneca Nation and Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation opposed it as an attempt to erase history/culture. Democrats planned legislation to reverse it. Scientists (International Association for Great Lakes Research) said they would continue using “Lake Ontario” with “no scientific or management justification” for change. Polling indicated majority U.S. opposition (around 71% of Americans, including many Republicans). Mapping services like MapQuest refused; Google searches still overwhelmingly favored the original name. Some Upstate New York Republicans also objected due to economic ties.[[3]](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-signs-order-rename-lake-ontario-lake-america-2026-08-27/)

**As of late August 2026 (latest available reports around August 29), the change is implemented for U.S. federal executive-branch purposes but rejected elsewhere, with no broader adoption and ongoing backlash.** U.S. agencies have updated official repositories and electronic documents (printed ones following). It does not bind Canada, U.S. states, international bodies, private companies, scientists, media, or the public—Canada maintains its own naming authority and Geographical Names Database. Weather forecasts, marine reports, and other non-federal U.S. sources continued using “Lake Ontario.” There is no single international authority to impose a name on shared waters (Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909 governs use, not names). The dispute remains a political/symbolic flashpoint in the trade tensions, with Democrats seeking reversal and no indication of Canadian or international concession. Private and public usage, plus scientific/international contexts, continue with the historic name.[[4]](https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/politics/2026/08/29/scientists-still-calling-it-lake-ontario-lake-america-trump-great-lakes/91518387007/)

As of today, there is **no official proposal, legislative bill, or serious political movement** to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The dispute you are referring to appears to be a **fringe, internet-driven idea** that has circulated in right-wing and nationalist social media circles, rather than a real policy debate.

Here is a breakdown of the situation, including who is floating the idea and why it has not gained traction:

### Who Is Proposing It?
The idea has been promoted by **minor social media influencers, meme pages, and a small contingent of nationalist commentators**—predominantly in the United States. The core argument is symbolic: they claim that since the U.S. holds the majority of the lake’s shoreline (the entire southern shore, while Canada holds the north), the name "Ontario" (which is the name of a Canadian province) is unfair. They propose "Lake America" to assert U.S. ownership and push back against perceived Canadian influence.

There is **no elected official, governor, member of Congress, or Canadian parliamentarian** who has introduced a formal resolution or bill to change the name. The U.S. Board on Geographic Names (BGN), the federal body that officially approves geographic names, has not received any petition on this matter.

### Who Is Objecting?
- **Canadian Officials and Citizens**: The proposal is seen as absurd and disrespectful. The name "Ontario" comes from the Iroquoian word *Skanadario* ("beautiful water" or "sparkling water") and predates both countries. Canada, which shares the lake, views the name as binational heritage.
- **Indigenous Communities**: The lake is sacred to several First Nations and Native American tribes (including the Haudenosaunee/Iroquois Confederacy). Any renaming would be seen as a colonial erasure of Indigenous history.
- **Geographers and Historians**: Experts point out that renaming a shared international waterway would require a treaty-level agreement between the U.S. and Canada under the International Boundary Commission, making it effectively impossible to do unilaterally.
- **Mainstream U.S. Politicians**: Both Democratic and Republican officials have ignored the idea. It is considered a distraction from actual issues, and no serious political figure wants to antagonize a close ally over a symbolic name.

### Current State of the Debate (as of Today)
- **Status: Dormant/Non-existent in official circles.** The debate exists only in the comment sections of social media posts and a few clickbait news articles from fringe outlets.
- **No legal mechanism is underway.** The BGN has strict rules against renaming geographic features without overwhelming local and state consent, and there is zero evidence of any such petition.
- **Public sentiment**: Polls do not track this issue, but the overwhelming consensus among Canadians and Americans who are aware of it is ridicule. It is often cited as an example of "online nationalism" that has no real-world policy impact.

**In short:** There is no active dispute to summarize because **no government body, governor, or major political party is pushing this**. It remains a viral rumor and a meme, not a real legislative fight. If you saw a news headline about it, it was likely satirical (e.g., *The Onion* style) or from a low-credibility website. The name "Lake Ontario" is legally and historically secure.

Within that shared scaffold there are discrepancies: anthropic states roughly 47% of the lake lies within the U.S. (implying the deepest/majority volume is American), while xai gives Canada 52-53% of the lake's surface; the two figures are not phrased consistently. Deepseek is equally confident but in the opposite direction, flatly asserting there is 'no official proposal, legislative bill, or serious political movement' and that any news of it is likely fringe or satirical, explicitly cautioning the reader that a headline they may have seen was probably not credible. None of the four 'event-confirming' responses hedge on whether the dispute is real, though they differ in how strongly they assert permanence (openai and anthropic describe it as 'official, effective immediately' at the federal level, while google and xai emphasize its provisional, contested, and non-binding nature outside U.S. federal agencies).
